case_info.scenario: A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"

       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Directly challenge the clinician to justify why scleroderma is prioritized over other fibrosing or seronegative conditions that also fit the presentation, such as RS3PE or eosinophilic fasciitis, given the absence of skin changes.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to

            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

Case:
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures.   B. Obtain a 3-phase bone scan
  C. Order anti-RNA polymerase III antibody testing
  D. Perform a full-thickness skin biopsy

The patient's significant tendon thickening and the contractures persisting despite steroid treatment further support scleroderma over these other conditions. Thus, I maintain that ordering the anti-RNA polymerase III antibody testing is the most appropriate next step.

[Doctor]: Thank you for your support. It's reassuring to have aligned reasoning on this. Let's proceed with ordering the anti-RNA polymerase III antibody testing to confirm or rule out systemic sclerosis. I'll also keep an eye on any evolving symptoms that might suggest other conditions, but for now, this seems like the most logical approach.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent. We are aligned in our diagnostic reasoning, and proceeding with anti-RNA polymerase III antibody testing is a focused and logical next step to evaluate for systemic sclerosis. I'll support this plan.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.
